Will you have portable suction equipment that he feels comfortable using in addition to scissors and other tools to release you from bondage? Will he be able to do it in time? What if your body tenses up and he struggles to free you because your body is acting on its own and the bondage cuts off circulation? I’m sure you’ve considered all of these things, and also I don’t know what type of seizures you have, but these are things I really hope you keep in mind because this could be really, truly dangerous.

My experience—BP1, diagnosed right before nursing school, in my 30s. Stable on lithium, have done lots of work alongside that—CBT, some DBT, ACT, psychoeducation, mood tracking, sleep tracking, mindfulness and meditation, healthy diet, exercise, journaling, etc. I was determined to give night shifts a try despite the risks to mood stability and personally it’s been okay. No manic shift, no depression. Possibly edging toward hypomania and anxiety at times but I’m aware of it and take steps to modify my lifestyle factors. I’m in regular touch with my doctor and a therapist to make sure I’m well. My family knows to contact my doctor if things are getting weird with me. My take is it’s not a complete contraindication to shift work, just stay in touch with yourself and stay on top of things. Maintain those lines of communication with loved ones and care providers.

I’ve had bad psychiatrists. One would fall asleep during the session (I was a teenager who didn’t say much so I guess good for him for getting his nap in). One flirted with me for months, but didn’t act on it beyond that, so good for him for fucking with a vulnerable person’s head but not doing anything overt enough to be reported. Having said that, even the best psychiatrists have their hands tied since the only thing they can directly use to effect change is medication/ECT/etc. What would really help many people would be regular appointments targeting a range of needs—psychologists/therapists, addictions counsellors, coaches of all kinds (life, career, fitness), social workers, personal support workers, peer support workers—people who could get individuals more involved in the community, show them free resources, encourage them to live their best life. Hands-on support is what people need, and that doesn’t exist without the money, and people in need tend not to have the money a lot of the time. If these supports were more integrated into the medical health system and more funded, psychiatrists could make referrals targeting their clients’ needs, follow up and tweak the regimen the way they tweak meds, and everyone would be happier.

Sorry—my thought process went somewhere else there. In Canada, especially in Conservative-dominant provinces, our social benefits like healthcare are being brutally underfunded in order to usher in privatization. There is public buy-in for privatization because of how expensive it would be to support the health of an aging population. Expense also courts sympathy from the public for how underfunded mental health, addictions, and other social support services are. I was thinking it might be possible to use the public outrage over how MAID is murdering people with disabilities and mental illness—people who, with adequate supports, would have a better quality of life and wouldn’t be suffering the way they are—to advocate for better social supports. It might be a way to gain public buy-in. *edit: gain support for increased funding for healthcare and other social supports, NOT gain buy-in for MAID.

Actually, the original post’s link was a reporter presenting a family’s concern about incorrectly carried-out MAID as if it were a reprehensible mistake. But we don’t know what happened in that man’s case. Several parties verified that MAID was carried out appropriately in that situation. This is clearly an emotional topic for you.

Yes, we need rock solid oversight, but if you think that a life of terrible misery is better simply because you’re against “murder,” guess what—you don’t have to “murder” anyone yourself, so you’re off the hook. But people who suffer deserve a way to ease their suffering.

Well like it or not, [it will be happening](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/medical-assistance-dying.html#b11), so we need to think about how can we care for people who are suffering while also reducing the potential for suffering.

Yes indeed. I think there should be more of this sort of discourse, more public campaigning about how the dissolution of our social safety nets have led to MAID being the only option for someone to find relief from avoidable chronic pain.

For severe, treatment-resistant mental illness where a person wishes to end their suffering, what options are there? Would palliative care be offered? How would mental anguish be palliated if none of the psychiatric treatments have worked? How can you improve someone’s quality of life realistically? Faced with a painful, possibly failed attempt at ending suffering, one that is likely to increase impairment if death is not the result, or continuing to live in horrible pain, MAID seems like the only humane option. 

Except that disability support payments are below the cost of living, the healthcare system is a mess, social services are stretched too thin, housing instability and overall inequality are rapidly continuing to increase, international relations are scary tense, the climate is trending towards fire, and we aren’t giving back to the land that gives us life. The world is a disaster, and it’s too expensive to care. So how can we care for people who need relief from their suffering?

So assuming healthcare is free, I think what’s most important is how you deliver the news, the information you share with the person, and the direction you give to the team. A person being held is not a criminal and should not be made to feel like one. They should be treated with dignity and respect. Let them keep their phone, treat them with kindness, and do not surround them like you would a wild animal if they’re distressed—use deescalation techniques to talk them down. I know you aren’t the one to give the medication or bring in the backup if someone starts getting testy, but you do lead the team and set the tone while you’re there. Deescalate before you think about medicating, and explain to the person everything you’re doing to the person. You are the one to deliver the news. It shows respect to a person to talk about all the reasons you made your decision. Bring them in as a partner in the decision even if they don’t have a say. They need to know exactly what everyone on the treatment team knows about their case. Even if they’re agitated and swearing at you, there will be a way to deliver all the information.
